To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a time‐domain whole‐filed fluorescence lifetime imaging (3D FLIIM) microscope with optical sectioning has been developed.

a new whole‐field FLIM microscope with optical sectioning has been developed that is based on the use of a mode‐locked, regeneratively amplified, Ti:Sapphire laser, a gated image intensifier combined to a gated intensified CCD camera and that it has been applied to the imaging and characterization of fluorescent dyes and biological tissue.
time‐domain whole‐area fluorescence lifetime imaging with the ability to perform optical section has been demonstrated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing new instrumentation for fluorescence lifetime imaging, with a view to improving the sensitivity and specificity of the technique for biological applications.
the development of whole‐field time domain FLIM microscopy for the study of tissue and other biological systems.

the development of a new generation of fluorescence lifetime microscopy (FLIM) instrumentation that is capable of high spatial and high temporal resolution and that is applicable to real‐world problems in biology and medicine.

the FLIM microscope presented in this paper is a powerful new tool for the quantitative study of fluorescence phenomena.
this FLIM instrument provides a new and powerful tool for the study of biological systems.
time‐domain whole‐ field FLIM with opticalsectioning is a powerful technique for quantitative chemical imaging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

this whole‐field time-domain fluorescence lifetime imaging (3D FLMI) microscope with optical sectioning has been demonstrated to be an extremely useful and flexible tool for the quantitative study of fluorescence lifetime.
we have demonstrated a whole‐field, optical sectioning, time‐domain FLIM microscope.
the whole‐field time domain fluorescence lifetime imaging with sectioning has been successfully developed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to obtain quantitative 3D images of fluorescence lifetime with a compact, portable and relatively inexpensive laser source.
the combination of time‐gated fluorescence imaging and structured illumination is a very promising route to compact 3D FLIM microscopy.
time‐domain whole‐file FLIM with optical-sectioning can be realized using compact, low cost, all-solid-state laser technology.
